 ELLIS HOBBS • UPDATED OCT. 21, 2026, 9:22 AM ET Reviewed by Jack Kellogg and Fact-checked by Tim Sykes Leverage Shares 2X Long SPCX Daily jumped as SPAC-related optimism surged, and its stocks have been trading up by 16.0 percent.
 Key Takeaways
 SPCH has slid from above $13 to the high-$9s, signaling a sharp momentum shift after an aggressive run.
 Daily candles show heavy intraday swings, highlighting how leveraged SPCH amplifies the underlying SPCX moves.
 Intraday tape points to tight consolidation around $10–$11, as traders battle over short-term direction.
 Lack of clear financial ratios keeps the focus squarely on price action and disciplined risk management.
 Active traders are watching prior support and resistance levels to frame potential day and swing trades.
 Live Update At 09:21:41 EDT: On Wednesday, October 21, 2026 Leverage Shares 2X Long SPCX Daily stock [BATS Global Markets: SPCH] is trending up by 16.0%! Discover the key drivers behind this movement as well as our expert analysis in the detailed breakdown below.
 Quick Financial Overview
 Leverage Shares 2X Long SPCX Daily, trading under ticker SPCH, is built as a trading product, not a classic fundamental story. The key ratios page is basically a blank slate. That tells traders one thing: SPCH is about price action, leverage, and short-term direction on its underlying, not earnings or balance sheets.
 Over the past few weeks, SPCH has traded roughly between $9 and $13, with a recent close near $9.41 after a high near $13.55 earlier in the month. That’s a big percentage swing in a short window. For traders, that means opportunity, but it also means real danger for anyone who over-sizes or overstays.

 The daily candles show wide ranges and frequent reversals. SPCH often gaps, spikes, and then retraces, typical of leveraged exchange-traded products. Since this is a 2X product, every move in the underlying is magnified on the SPCH chart, both up and down. Without earnings, dividends, or valuation anchors, traders must lean on chart levels, volume, and volatility bands to navigate this name.
 Why Traders Are Watching SPCH Price Action
 SPCH has been delivering the kind of intraday swings that attract momentum traders. Earlier this month, SPCH ripped from around $9.80 to over $12.90 in a handful of sessions, a move of more than 30%. Since then, it has backed off toward the mid-$9s, showing how quickly leveraged products can round-trip gains.
 The daily chart of SPCH looks like a series of mini rollercoasters. One day it opens near $11.80, pushes above $12, then closes lower around $11.57. Another day it taps the mid-$13s before fading. This pattern tells experienced traders that SPCH is a textbook “trade the move, not the story” vehicle. The story here is leverage — nothing more, nothing less.
 Zoom in to the intraday five-minute chart and the message is the same. SPCH spends long stretches chopping between $10.80 and $11.10, then throws quick pushes to $11.18 or dips into the $10.70s. Those 3–4% intraday swings become fuel for scalpers and short-term breakout traders.
 Because SPCH tracks a SPAC-focused product with 2X leverage, broad sentiment toward speculative growth and SPAC exposure can hit it fast. When risk-on flows return to that corner of the market, SPCH tends to react aggressively. When traders de-risk, the selling pressure can be just as violent. For now, the tape shows a recent downtrend from the $13 area but with active two-sided trading around $10–$11, a clear battleground for short-term setups.
 Conclusion
 For active traders, SPCH is a pure volatility play. With no meaningful revenue, margin, or debt metrics to anchor long-term valuations, Leverage Shares 2X Long SPCX Daily trades like a levered sentiment gauge on a SPAC-heavy basket. The recent slide from the $13s to under $10 is not a quiet drift; it’s a sharp reset that punishes late chasers and rewards traders who respected prior resistance.
 Intraday, SPCH continues to show steady liquidity and tight ranges that occasionally explode into fast moves. Those pops above $11 and flushes into the high-$10s are where disciplined traders find their edge, using clear risk levels and tight stops. The daily support band around $9–$9.20, and resistance zones near $11.50–$12, are the obvious levels on most screens.
 The key with SPCH is remembering what it is: a leveraged tool. That demands strict rules. As Tim Sykes loves to hammer home, “The market doesn’t owe you anything — trade the pattern, cut losses quickly, and don’t fall in love with any ticker.” As millionaire penny stock trader and teacher Tim Sykes, says, “It’s better to go home at zero than to go home in the red.”. For traders using SPCH, that mindset isn’t optional. It’s survival. This analysis is for educational and research purposes only, and every trader needs a plan before touching a product that can move this fast.

 The available research on day trading suggests that most active traders lose money. Fees and overtrading are major contributors to these losses. 
 A 2000 study called “Trading is Hazardous to Your Wealth: The Common Stock Investment Performance of Individual Investors” evaluated 66,465 U.S. households that held stocks from 1991 to 1996. The households that traded most averaged an 11.4% annual return during a period where the overall market gained 17.9%. These lower returns were attributed to overconfidence. 
 A 2014 paper (revised 2019) titled “Learning Fast or Slow?” analyzed the complete transaction history of the Taiwan Stock Exchange between 1992 and 2006. It looked at the ongoing performance of day traders in this sample, and found that 97% of day traders can expect to lose money from trading, and more than 90% of all day trading volume can be traced to investors who predictably lose money. Additionally, it tied the behavior of gamblers and drivers who get more speeding tickets to overtrading, and cited studies showing that legalized gambling has an inverse effect on trading volume. 
 A 2019 research study (revised 2020) called “Day Trading for a Living?” observed 19,646 Brazilian futures contract traders who started day trading from 2013 to 2015, and recorded two years of their trading activity. The study authors found that 97% of traders with more than 300 days actively trading lost money, and only 1.1% earned more than the Brazilian minimum wage ($16 USD per day). They hypothesized that the greater returns shown in previous studies did not differentiate between frequent day traders and those who traded rarely, and that more frequent trading activity decreases the chance of profitability. 
 These studies show the wide variance of the available data on day trading profitability. One thing that seems clear from the research is that most day traders lose money .
